name: Glycogen storage disease type IX (phosphorylase kinase)

clinicalPearls: GSD IX results from deficiency of phosphorylase kinase, the enzyme that activates glycogen phosphorylase, and is one of the commonest glycogen storage diseases
It is genetically heterogeneous: the frequent X-linked liver form is caused by PHKA2, while PHKB, PHKG2, and PHKA1 variants give other liver or muscle phenotypes
The typical liver phenotype presents in early childhood with hepatomegaly, growth delay, and mild fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia, closely resembling Hers disease (GSD VI)
Biochemistry usually shows fasting ketosis with mild hypoglycaemia and normal or only mildly elevated lactate and uric acid
The X-linked liver form (PHKA2) is often mild and tends to improve with age, whereas PHKG2-related disease carries a higher risk of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis
A muscle form (PHKA1) causes exercise intolerance, cramps, and myoglobinuria rather than hepatic disease
Management of the liver forms is dietary, avoiding fasting and using cornstarch, with monitoring for hepatic complications
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphorylase kinase is a multi-subunit enzyme that activates glycogen phosphorylase by phosphorylation, enabling glycogenolysis. In GSD IX, variants in the genes encoding its subunits (PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2 in liver; PHKA1 in muscle) reduce kinase activity, so glycogen phosphorylase remains inadequately activated and glycogen breakdown is impaired. In the liver this causes glycogen accumulation and hepatomegaly with mild fasting hypoglycaemia and ketosis, generally milder than GSD I because gluconeogenesis is intact. In muscle, deficient glycogenolysis limits energy supply during exertion, producing exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Hers disease (GSD VI, liver phosphorylase deficiency)
Other hepatic glycogen storage diseases (GSD I, III, 0)
McArdle disease and other muscle glycogenoses in the muscle form
Other causes of childhood hepatomegaly and growth delay
additionalInvestigations: Fasting studies showing mild ketotic hypoglycaemia with near-normal lactate and uric acid
Molecular genetic testing of PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2, and PHKA1
Phosphorylase kinase enzyme activity assay in blood cells, liver, or muscle
Liver ultrasound to assess hepatomegaly and monitor for fibrosis, especially in PHKG2 disease
Creatine kinase and exercise assessment in the muscle form
redFlags: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or altered consciousness
Signs of progressive hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis, particularly in PHKG2-related disease
Exertional myoglobinuria or rhabdomyolysis in the muscle form
reference.prognosis: Most liver forms, especially the X-linked PHKA2 subtype, are mild and improve with age with a good long-term outlook; PHKG2-related disease has a higher risk of cirrhosis and requires closer surveillance, while the muscle form causes variable exercise limitation.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish GSD IX from GSD VI, which requires enzymology or genetics
Assuming all subtypes are benign and not monitoring PHKG2 disease for cirrhosis
Overlooking the X-linked inheritance pattern in the common PHKA2 form during counselling
Missing the muscle phenotype in a patient presenting with exercise intolerance rather than liver disease
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: In the liver form, prevent ketotic hypoglycaemia with frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch while avoiding prolonged fasting
Provide adequate dietary protein and calories to support growth and gluconeogenesis under dietitian supervision
Give an emergency glucose regimen during illness or fasting to avert hypoglycaemia
In the muscle form (PHKA1), advise pacing of exertion and avoidance of intense anaerobic exercise to prevent cramps and myoglobinuria
Monitor growth, liver biochemistry, fasting glucose and ketones, with hepatic ultrasound and fibrosis assessment in PHKG2 disease
Refer to metabolic medicine and hepatology, and offer genetic counselling and family screening for X-linked and autosomal recessive subtypes
